short: The system of rules, practices and checks that decides how a company is directed and controlled, and in whose interest.
kid: When friends run a lemonade stand together, they agree on who decides what, and they check each other's counting. Fair rules stop anyone from taking more than their share.
detail: Corporate governance is the framework of rules, relationships and processes through which a company is directed and controlled. It covers the board and its committees, shareholder rights, disclosure and audit, executive pay, and how conflicts between managers, controlling owners, minority investors and lenders are handled. In India the main rules come from the Companies Act, 2013 and SEBI's LODR regulations, shaped by the Kumar Mangalam Birla (1999), Narayana Murthy (2003) and Uday Kotak (2017) committees. Because most Indian listed firms have a controlling promoter, the central risk is less about managers ignoring owners and more about promoters favouring themselves over minority shareholders. Good governance tends to lower a company's cost of capital and the risk of blow-ups. The common confusion: ticking every compliance box is not the same as good governance; Satyam met the formal board rules before its fraud came to light in 2009.
example: Say two companies each earn ₹100 crore a year. Investors trust ABC Ltd's independent board and clean disclosures and value it at 25 times earnings, or ₹2,500 crore, while doubts over XYZ Ltd's related-party deals hold it to 15 times, or ₹1,500 crore. The ₹1,000 crore gap is the market's discount for weaker governance.

short: The group of people elected by shareholders to oversee a company's management, set its direction and protect the owners' interests.
kid: A board is like the group of grown-ups who look after a school club. They do not run every game, but they choose the leader and make sure things are done fairly.
detail: The board of directors is the body elected by shareholders to govern a company. It appoints and can remove the chief executive, approves strategy, budgets, large investments, dividends and the financial statements, and oversees risk and compliance through committees such as audit, nomination and remuneration, and stakeholder relationship. Under India's Companies Act, 2013, as of 2025 a public company needs at least three directors and a private company two, the board must meet at least four times a year with no more than 120 days between meetings, and directors owe duties of care and loyalty under Section 166. Listed companies must also have a woman director and, under SEBI's LODR rules, a minimum share of independent directors. The common confusion: the board does not run day-to-day operations; it supervises the managers who do, and a board that merely rubber-stamps management fails at its job.
example: Say ABC Ltd has 10 directors: 3 executives, including an executive chairperson, 2 promoter nominees and 5 independent directors. With an executive chairperson, LODR requires at least half the board, 5 of 10, to be independent, so ABC just meets the rule; if one independent director resigns, it drops to 4 of 10 and must appoint a replacement.

short: A board member with no significant financial or family ties to the company, its promoters or its managers, appointed to give unbiased oversight.
kid: When two friends argue over sharing toys, a kind neighbour who is on neither side listens to both. The neighbour helps them decide what is fair.
detail: An independent director is a non-executive board member with no material relationship with the company, its promoters, its managers or their relatives, apart from sitting fees and profit-linked commission; they cannot receive stock options. Their job is to protect minority shareholders, lead key committees such as audit and nomination and remuneration, and question related-party deals and management decisions. Under the Companies Act, 2013 and SEBI's LODR rules as of 2025, at least one-third of a listed company's board must be independent, rising to half when the chairperson is an executive or linked to the promoter. They serve at most two five-year terms, the second needing a special resolution, and must pass an online proficiency test unless exempted by experience. The common confusion: non-executive does not mean independent; a promoter's nominee or a recent former employee may be non-executive but is not independent.
example: Say ABC Ltd has a board of 9 and a non-executive chairperson who has no link to the promoter. LODR then requires at least one-third, or 3, independent directors. If the chairperson were the promoter's brother instead, at least half the board would have to be independent, and since 4 is less than half of 9, ABC would need 5.

short: A board member who does not work in the company's day-to-day management, unlike an executive director such as the managing director.
kid: Some helpers at a lemonade stand squeeze lemons every day. Others just visit now and then to give advice and check that things are fair.
detail: Directors fall into two groups. Executive directors work full-time in the business: the managing director (MD), who is entrusted with substantial powers of management, and whole-time directors, who are in the company's full-time employment, such as a finance or operations director. Non-executive directors (NEDs) attend board and committee meetings but hold no management role, and are paid sitting fees and sometimes a commission from profits rather than a salary. NEDs include independent directors and non-independent ones, such as nominees of promoters, lenders or private equity investors. Their value lies in outside perspective and the freedom to challenge management. Under SEBI's LODR rules as of 2025, at least half of a listed company's board must be non-executive. The common confusion: non-executive does not mean independent; a promoter's relative on the board may be non-executive yet clearly not independent.
example: Say ABC Ltd has 8 directors: a managing director, 2 whole-time directors, 1 promoter nominee and 4 independent directors. That is 3 executive and 5 non-executive directors, so 5 of 8, or 62.5%, are non-executive, above LODR's 50% minimum, while 4 of 8 are independent.

short: The top officers Indian company law treats as a company's key managers: its chief executive or managing director, whole-time directors, finance chief and company secretary.
kid: In a school, the head teacher, the person who looks after the money and the person who keeps the rule book are the most important helpers. A big shop has helpers like these too.
detail: Key managerial personnel (KMP) is a legal category under Section 2(51) of the Companies Act, 2013. It covers the chief executive officer (CEO) or managing director or manager, the company secretary (CS), whole-time directors, the chief financial officer (CFO) and other senior officers the board designates. Listed companies, and public companies with paid-up capital of ₹10 crore or more, must appoint whole-time KMP. A vacancy must be filled within six months under the Act, and within three months for listed companies under SEBI's LODR rules as of 2025. The CEO leads the business, the CFO certifies the financial statements along with the CEO, and the CS runs board processes and compliance. KMP pay must be disclosed in the annual report, and KMP count as related parties. The common confusion: KMP is a legal label, not every senior manager; a head of sales is not KMP unless designated.
example: Say ABC Ltd's CEO, who is also a director, is paid ₹6 crore this year against ₹5 crore last year, while the median employee earns ₹8 lakh. The annual report must show his 20% pay rise, as it must for every KMP, and, because he sits on the board, a pay ratio of 75 times the median employee.

short: A board committee, mostly of independent directors, that oversees a company's financial reporting, auditors, internal controls and related-party deals.
kid: Before the class shares how many sweets are in the jar, a small group of fair helpers checks the counting and asks questions.
detail: The audit committee is a board committee that supervises financial reporting and the audit. It reviews quarterly and annual results before the board approves them, recommends the appointment and pay of the statutory auditor, oversees internal audit and internal financial controls, approves related-party transactions and runs the whistle-blower mechanism. Under Section 177 of the Companies Act, 2013 and Regulation 18 of SEBI's LODR rules as of 2025, a listed company's audit committee needs at least three directors, two-thirds of them independent, an independent chairperson, members who are all financially literate and at least one with accounting or financial expertise. It must meet at least four times a year. It matters because it is the board's main defence against misreporting. The common confusion: the audit committee does not audit the books itself; it oversees the auditors and managers who do that work.
example: Say ABC Ltd's audit committee has 3 members, 2 of them independent. That meets the two-thirds rule exactly, provided the chairperson is one of the 2 independent members. If the committee grows to 5, it needs at least 4 independent members, because 3 out of 5 is only 60%, short of two-thirds.

short: The total pay of a company's top executives, including salary, bonuses, stock awards and perks, and the way it is set and approved.
kid: The captain of a team gets a reward when the team does well. Everyone wants the reward to be fair, not too big, and given only for good work.
detail: Executive compensation is everything a company pays its senior leaders: fixed salary, annual bonus or profit commission, long-term incentives such as stock options or performance shares, retirement benefits and perks. Good design links pay to long-run shareholder value, easing the agency problem; bad design rewards short-term results or excessive risk. In India a nomination and remuneration committee recommends pay, and Section 197 of the Companies Act, 2013 caps a public company's total managerial remuneration at 11% of net profit, with 5% for any one managing or whole-time director, unless shareholders approve more by special resolution, under the rules as of 2025. The US Dodd-Frank Act of 2010 introduced a non-binding 'say on pay' shareholder vote. The common confusion: headline pay figures often include stock awards valued when granted, which the executive may never receive in full.
example: Say ABC Ltd, a public company, has net profit of ₹400 crore as computed under the Companies Act. Total pay to its directors and manager is capped at 11%, or ₹44 crore, and pay to a single managing director at 5%, or ₹20 crore. Paying the managing director ₹26 crore would need shareholders to pass a special resolution.

short: A rule that lets a company take back pay already given, such as bonuses based on profits later found to be wrong.
kid: If you got a prize sweet for winning a race, but later everyone saw you took a shortcut, you would have to give the sweet back.
detail: A clawback is a contractual or legal right to recover pay that has already been handed out, usually because it was based on results later restated or because of misconduct. A related tool, malus, cancels or cuts deferred pay before it vests. In the US, SEC Rule 10D-1, adopted under the Dodd-Frank Act and enforced through exchange listing rules from late 2023, requires listed companies to recover incentive pay wrongly awarded in the three years before an accounting restatement, regardless of fault. In India, RBI rules require private and foreign banks to apply malus and clawback to the variable pay of senior staff. In private equity, a GP clawback makes the general partner return carried interest if, at the end of the fund, it has received more than its agreed share of profits. The common confusion: clawback recovers money already paid; malus stops money not yet paid.
example: Say ABC Inc pays its CEO a $3 million bonus based on reported profit of $200 million. A restatement later cuts that profit to $150 million, which under the bonus formula would have earned only $1.8 million. Under a clawback policy, the company must recover the $1.2 million difference.

short: A deal between a company and someone close to it, such as its promoter, directors, their relatives or group companies.
kid: If the lemonade stand buys lemons from the owner's own brother, everyone wants to check the price is fair. Otherwise the brother might get too many coins.
detail: A related-party transaction (RPT) is any transfer of goods, services, assets or money between a company and a related party: its promoters, directors, key managerial personnel, their relatives, or entities they control, including subsidiaries and group firms. RPTs are legal and often sensible, such as buying from a group supplier, but they create the risk that value is shifted to insiders. Indian rules therefore require audit committee approval, disclosure and arm's-length pricing. Under SEBI's LODR rules as of 2025, material RPTs, those above a size threshold SEBI revises from time to time, need prior shareholder approval in which no related party may vote in favour, which works like a majority-of-minority vote. Ind AS 24 sets the disclosure rules in financial statements. The common confusion: a large RPT is not proof of wrongdoing; the questions are whether the price is fair and whether minority shareholders had a real say.
example: Say a promoter holds 60% of ABC Ltd and public investors hold 40%. ABC proposes a material purchase from the promoter's private firm, so only unrelated shareholders can vote for it. If holders of 30% of the shares vote, 12% for and 18% against, the resolution fails, even though the promoter alone owns 60%.

short: When a company's controlling owner shifts money or assets out of it for personal benefit, at the expense of minority shareholders.
kid: Imagine a shared toy box for the whole class. One child secretly carries the best toys home, a few at a time, so the box quietly empties for everyone else.
detail: Tunnelling, a term popularised by economists Simon Johnson, Rafael La Porta, Florencio Lopez-de-Silanes and Andrei Shleifer in 2000, is the transfer of resources out of a firm to its controlling shareholders. It works through overpriced purchases from, or cheap sales to, promoter-owned firms; loans and guarantees to group companies that are never repaid; excessive royalties or brand fees; and share issues that dilute minority holders. Pyramid-shaped business groups, common in India and East Asia, make it easier because a promoter may own all of one firm but only 30% of another. Regulators respond with related-party rules, independent directors and forensic audits. The common confusion: tunnelling is often dressed up as ordinary business and may be technically legal, which is why it is hard to prove and why Indian siphoning cases usually surface only after a forensic audit.
example: Say a promoter owns 40% of listed ABC Ltd and 100% of a private supplier. ABC buys goods worth ₹100 crore from the supplier for ₹130 crore, cutting ABC's profit by ₹30 crore. The promoter loses 40% of that, ₹12 crore, through ABC but gains the full ₹30 crore through the supplier, so he is ₹18 crore richer and minority shareholders are ₹18 crore poorer.

short: Buying or selling a company's securities while holding important information about it that the public does not yet have.
kid: If you peeked at the answers before a quiz and then made a bet on who would win, that would not be fair to the others.
detail: Insider trading is dealing in a listed company's securities while in possession of material information that is not public, or passing such information to others who trade. In India it is prohibited by SEBI's PIT regulations, which call such information unpublished price sensitive information (UPSI); in the US it is prosecuted mainly under SEC Rule 10b-5, made under the Securities Exchange Act of 1934. The ban covers not only directors and employees but auditors, bankers, lawyers, relatives and anyone tipped off. It matters because markets work only if investors believe they are not trading against people who already know the answer. Penalties include disgorgement, fines, trading bans and prison; Galleon founder Raj Rajaratnam was sentenced to 11 years in the US in 2011. The common confusion: insiders may legally trade their own company's shares when they hold no UPSI, respect trading windows and disclose their trades.
example: Say a banker advising on a takeover tells a friend that XYZ Ltd will be bought at ₹600 a share. The friend buys 5,000 shares at ₹450, or ₹22.5 lakh, and after the announcement the price rises to ₹590, a gain of ₹7 lakh. Both have broken insider trading rules, the friend by trading and the banker by passing on the information, even though the banker never traded.

short: Non-public information about a listed company that would likely move its share price once released, such as results or a merger.
kid: It is a secret about a toy shop, like a big new toy arriving next week, that would make everyone rush to the shop if they knew.
detail: Unpublished price sensitive information (UPSI) is the central idea in SEBI's Prohibition of Insider Trading Regulations, 2015. It means information about a company or its securities that is not generally available and that, once public, is likely to materially affect the price; the US equivalent is material non-public information. The rules list typical examples: financial results, dividends, changes in capital structure, mergers, demergers, acquisitions, delistings and disposals, and changes in key managerial personnel, and SEBI has widened the list over time. Companies may share UPSI only for legitimate purposes, must log every recipient in a structured digital database, and close the trading window for designated persons from the end of each quarter until 48 hours after results. The common confusion: rumours, analyst estimates and conclusions drawn from public data are not UPSI, so trading on careful research is legal.
example: Say ABC Ltd's board approves a buyback at ₹1,200 a share while the stock trades at ₹1,000. Until the decision reaches the stock exchanges, that 20% premium is UPSI, and a director's relative who buys 1,000 shares for ₹10 lakh before the announcement risks a SEBI insider trading case, however small the trade.

short: Illegally trading ahead of a large client order you know about, to profit from the price move that order will cause.
kid: If you know your friend is about to buy lots of ice creams, you rush in first, buy some, then sell them to your friend for more. That is not fair.
detail: Front running is trading for your own account, or tipping others, using advance knowledge of a large pending order from a client or fund that is likely to move the price. A dealer who knows a mutual fund is about to buy a big block of shares can buy first and then sell into the fund's buying at a higher price, profiting at the client's expense. It breaches the duty owed to clients and is prohibited in India under SEBI's PFUTP regulations. After cases involving dealers at fund houses, notably Axis Mutual Fund in 2022, SEBI required asset managers to build systems to detect and deter it. The term is also used loosely for traders buying ahead of predictable public events such as index rebalancing, which is legal. The common confusion: front running depends on private knowledge of someone else's order, not on a clever forecast.
example: Say a dealer learns that his fund house will buy 10 lakh shares of ABC Ltd. He buys 50,000 shares at ₹300 through a friend's account, the fund's buying lifts the price to ₹312, and he sells. His illegal gain is 50,000 × ₹12 = ₹6 lakh, and the fund paid more for its shares.

short: Deliberately distorting a security's price or trading activity to mislead other investors, for example through fake trades or false tips.
kid: A child whispers that a plain marble is super rare, so friends pay lots for it, and he sells them his own marbles. Later everyone finds out it was just an ordinary marble.
detail: Market manipulation is any scheme that creates a false or misleading picture of a security's price, demand or trading volume. Common forms are pump and dump (hyping a thinly traded stock, then selling to the buyers it attracts), circular trading and wash trades among linked accounts to fake volume, spoofing (placing large orders with no intention of letting them execute), marking the close and spreading false news. In India it is banned by SEBI's Prohibition of Fraudulent and Unfair Trade Practices (PFUTP) Regulations, 2003, and SEBI has acted against stock-tip channels on Telegram and YouTube. In the US, the Dodd-Frank Act explicitly outlawed spoofing in commodity futures markets, and the CFA Institute's Standard II(B) forbids manipulation by its members. Manipulated prices misallocate capital and drive honest investors away. The common confusion: buying heavily because you believe in a stock is not manipulation; intent to mislead is.
example: Say operators quietly buy 20 lakh shares of a tiny company at ₹10, spending ₹2 crore, then flood chat groups with tips until the price reaches ₹35. They sell everything for ₹7 crore, a ₹5 crore profit, and once their selling ends the price collapses to ₹8, leaving late buyers with heavy losses.

short: A situation where a person's own interests could pull them away from acting fairly for the people they are supposed to serve.
kid: If you are the judge of a drawing contest and your best friend enters, it is hard to be fair. You should tell everyone, or let someone else judge.
detail: A conflict of interest arises when a person or firm owes a duty to someone, such as a client, employer or shareholders, but has a personal or business interest that could bias their judgement. Examples include an analyst rating a stock that her employer is helping to sell, a distributor pushing the fund that pays the highest commission, a director voting on a contract with a relative's firm, or a rating agency paid by the issuer it rates. Conflicts cannot always be removed, so the usual tools are disclosure, recusal, separating teams with information barriers and client-first rules. Indian directors must disclose their interests under Section 184 of the Companies Act, 2013, SEBI requires analysts and advisers to disclose holdings and fees, and CFA Institute Standard VI(A) demands the same. The common confusion: having a conflict is not itself wrongdoing; hiding it or acting on it is.
example: Say a distributor can sell you Fund A, which pays him a 1% trail commission a year, or a similar Fund B, which pays 0.4%. On your ₹20 lakh investment, recommending Fund A earns him ₹20,000 a year instead of ₹8,000, a ₹12,000 reason to favour it that he should disclose.

short: A legal duty to act in someone else's best interest, with loyalty and care, when you manage their money or affairs.
kid: When a friend asks you to hold their piggy bank while they play, you keep it safe and never take a coin. You look after it as if it were your own.
detail: A fiduciary duty is the highest standard of legal obligation, owed by someone trusted to act for another person, the beneficiary. It has two main parts: the duty of loyalty (put the beneficiary first, avoid or disclose conflicts, never profit secretly) and the duty of care (act with the diligence and skill a prudent person would use). Company directors owe fiduciary duties to the company and its stakeholders, set out in India in Section 166 of the Companies Act, 2013; trustees, fund managers and SEBI-registered investment advisers owe similar duties to investors. Courts usually give directors leeway for honest business decisions that turn out badly, an idea called the business judgement rule. The common confusion: many people who sell financial products, such as distributors and insurance agents, are not fiduciaries, so their advice need not be in your best interest.
example: Say the directors of ABC Ltd approve selling a factory to a company owned by the chairperson's son for ₹60 crore, ignoring an independent valuation of ₹80 crore and a rival bid of ₹75 crore. Shareholders lose at least ₹15 crore compared with the best offer, and the directors have likely breached their duty of loyalty.

short: A firm that studies the resolutions at shareholder meetings and recommends to institutional investors how to vote on them.
kid: Before a class vote, a helper reads all the choices carefully and tells busy friends which one seems best. The friends still choose for themselves.
detail: A proxy advisory firm researches the resolutions put to shareholders, such as director appointments, executive pay, related-party deals and mergers, and publishes voting recommendations for institutional investors, which often hold hundreds of companies and cannot study every meeting. Globally the two largest are Institutional Shareholder Services (ISS) and Glass Lewis; in India the main ones are Institutional Investor Advisory Services (IiAS), InGovern and Stakeholders Empowerment Services. SEBI regulates them under its research analyst rules and requires them to publish their voting policies and share reports with the company. Their influence is large because mutual funds, insurers and foreign investors often follow their advice, so an 'against' recommendation can sink a special resolution. Critics say they wield power without owning shares and apply one-size-fits-all rules. The common confusion: proxy advisers do not vote; the investors they advise do.
example: Say ABC Ltd needs a special resolution, which passes only if votes for are at least three times the votes against. The promoter votes its 45% of the shares for, and other holders cast 10% for. If institutions holding 20% follow a proxy adviser's 'against' advice, the tally is 55 for and 20 against; since 55 is less than 3 × 20 = 60, the resolution fails.

short: When investors use their shareholding to push a company's management to change strategy, governance, payouts or leadership.
kid: If some friends who chipped in for a lemonade stand think it is run badly, they speak up and ask for changes. Sometimes they even ask for a new person in charge.
detail: Shareholder activism is the use of an ownership stake to influence how a company is run. Activists, often hedge funds such as Elliott Management or Trian Partners, build a stake and then push for changes: selling a division, returning cash through buybacks, cutting costs, replacing directors or the CEO, or blocking a merger. Tactics range from private letters and public campaigns to proxy fights for board seats. Under India's Companies Act, 2013, holders of at least 10% of the voting capital can requisition an extraordinary general meeting, which Invesco attempted at Zee Entertainment in 2021. Activism can also target environmental or social issues, and stewardship codes have pushed Indian institutions to vote more actively. Activists argue they fix underperformance; critics say some chase quick gains. The common confusion: activism is not a hostile takeover; activists usually want change, not control.
example: Say an activist fund buys 5% of ABC Inc, worth $500 million when the company's market value is $10 billion. It persuades the board to sell a loss-making unit and buy back shares, and the stock rises 20%. The activist's stake is now worth $600 million, a $100 million gain.

short: Shareholders who do not control a company, because their stake is too small to decide board seats or major votes on its own.
kid: When a big kid owns most of the toys in a shared box, the smaller kids still own some. Rules make sure the big kid cannot simply take theirs away.
detail: Minority shareholders are owners without a controlling stake. In India, where promoters often hold half or more of a listed company, public investors are usually the minority, and their main risk is that the controller uses the company for private benefit, for example through related-party deals or unfair mergers. Indian law offers several protections: special resolutions need three times as many votes for as against, material related-party deals need approval without promoter votes, the takeover code forces an open offer when control changes, and listed companies must keep at least 25% public shareholding. Under Sections 241 to 244 of the Companies Act, 2013, shareholders can petition the NCLT against oppression and mismanagement, as the Mistry family did against Tata Sons in 2016; the Supreme Court ruled for Tata Sons in 2021. The common confusion: minority does not mean powerless; minority votes often decide contested resolutions.
example: Say ABC Pvt Ltd has issued 10 lakh shares held by 1,200 shareholders. An oppression and mismanagement petition can be filed by members holding at least 1 lakh shares (10%), or by at least 100 members, because 100 is fewer than one-tenth of 1,200, which is 120.

short: A share structure in which some shares carry more votes than others, letting founders keep control while owning a smaller economic stake.
kid: Imagine a club where the child who started it gets ten votes and everyone else gets one. The starter keeps deciding the games even when lots of new friends join.
detail: A dual-class structure issues shares with unequal voting rights but usually equal claims on profits. Founders hold high-vote shares and public investors buy low- or no-vote shares, so founders keep control after raising large amounts of equity; Alphabet and Meta are well-known US examples. In India, Tata Motors issued shares with differential voting rights (DVRs) in 2008, carrying one vote per ten shares and a higher dividend, and folded them back into ordinary shares in 2024. Since 2019 SEBI has allowed tech-led companies to list with superior voting rights (SR) shares held by founders, subject, under the rules as of 2025, to at most 10 votes per share, a sunset clause and one vote per share on key matters. Supporters say this protects long-term vision; critics say it entrenches founders. The common confusion: these are ordinary equity shares, not preference shares.
example: Say the founders of ABC Inc hold 10 million Class B shares with 10 votes each, while investors hold 90 million Class A shares with one vote each. The founders own 10 of 100 million shares, or 10% of the economic interest, but cast 100 million of 190 million votes, about 52.6%, enough to control every ordinary vote.

short: The yearly meeting at which a company's shareholders receive the accounts, vote on dividends, directors and auditors, and question the board.
kid: Once a year, everyone who chipped in for the lemonade stand meets up. They hear how it went, share the extra coins and choose who will help run it next year.
detail: An annual general meeting (AGM) is the yearly meeting of a company's shareholders required by company law. Under Section 96 of India's Companies Act, 2013, it must be held within six months of the end of the financial year, with no more than 15 months between two AGMs, and needs at least 21 clear days' notice. Ordinary business is adopting the financial statements, declaring dividends, reappointing directors who retire by rotation and appointing auditors; anything else is special business. Any other shareholder meeting is an extraordinary general meeting (EGM), called for matters such as a merger or a fund-raise, and holders of 10% of the voting capital can demand one. Listed companies must offer e-voting, and under relaxations in force as of 2025 many meet by video conference. The common confusion: most votes are cast electronically before the meeting, so the AGM is more about questions than voting.
example: Say ABC Ltd's financial year ends on 31 March 2026 and its last AGM was on 20 August 2025. The six-month rule requires the next AGM by 30 September 2026, earlier than the 15-month limit of 20 November 2026, so 30 September is the deadline, and notice must go out at least 21 clear days before the meeting.

short: A formal decision put to a company's shareholders for a vote, passed as an ordinary or special resolution depending on the matter.
kid: When friends who share a toy box want to change a rule, they raise their hands. Small changes need more hands up than down, and big changes need many more.
detail: A shareholder resolution is a proposal voted on by a company's members at a general meeting or through a postal ballot. Under Section 114 of India's Companies Act, 2013, an ordinary resolution passes when votes for exceed votes against, and covers routine matters such as adopting accounts, declaring dividends and appointing directors and auditors. A special resolution needs votes for of at least three times the votes against, effectively 75% of votes cast, and is required for weightier decisions such as amending the articles, a preferential share issue, a large buyback or reappointing an independent director. A postal ballot, now mostly electronic, lets shareholders vote without a meeting. In the US, 'shareholder resolution' usually means a proposal filed by shareholders themselves, for instance on climate or pay. The common confusion: only votes cast count; shares that abstain or do not vote are ignored.
example: Say 50 crore votes are cast: 37 crore for and 13 crore against. As an ordinary resolution it passes easily, but as a special resolution it fails, because 37 crore is less than 3 × 13 crore = 39 crore. If just 50 lakh votes switched from against to for, the tally of 37.5 crore to 12.5 crore would meet the test exactly.
formula: Special resolution passes if: Votes for ≥ 3 × Votes against

short: India's accounting standards, closely based on the international IFRS rules, which listed and larger Indian companies must follow in their financial statements.
kid: Every child in a class counts their marbles the same way, so anyone can compare. Big shops in India also share one counting rulebook like that.
detail: Indian Accounting Standards (Ind AS) are the accounting standards notified by the Ministry of Corporate Affairs under the Companies (Indian Accounting Standards) Rules, 2015, drafted by the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India. They are converged with IFRS rather than copied word for word, so each Ind AS mirrors an IFRS or IAS standard, such as Ind AS 116 for IFRS 16, with a few Indian carve-outs. They became mandatory in phases from 1 April 2016, first for companies with net worth of ₹500 crore or more, then for all listed companies and larger unlisted ones, and later for most NBFCs; smaller companies still use the older Indian GAAP standards. As of 2025, banks and insurers had not yet moved their main accounts to Ind AS. The common confusion: Ind AS figures are not directly comparable with a company's older Indian GAAP numbers.
example: Say ABC Ltd leases a warehouse for 5 years at ₹10 crore a year, paid at each year-end, and its borrowing rate is 8%. Under Ind AS 116 it records a lease liability, and a matching right-of-use asset, equal to the present value of the payments, about ₹39.93 crore, instead of simply expensing ₹10 crore of rent each year as under the old Indian GAAP rules.

short: The global accounting rulebook, set by the International Accounting Standards Board, used by listed companies in most countries outside the US.
kid: Children in many countries agree to count their sweets the same way, so a child in one country can understand another child's count. Big shops in many countries share one counting rulebook too.
detail: International Financial Reporting Standards (IFRS) are accounting standards issued by the International Accounting Standards Board (IASB), an independent body overseen by the IFRS Foundation in London. Standards issued by its predecessor before 2001 are called International Accounting Standards (IAS), and many, such as IAS 16 on property and IAS 36 on impairment, remain in force. More than 140 jurisdictions require IFRS for all or most listed companies, including the EU, UK, Australia and Canada, and India adapted them as Ind AS. IFRS is usually described as more principles-based than US GAAP; notable differences include IFRS's ban on LIFO inventory costing and its capitalisation of qualifying development costs. In 2023 the foundation's sister board, the ISSB, issued its first sustainability disclosure standards. The common confusion: US domestic companies do not use IFRS, though foreign companies listed in the US may file under it.
example: Say ABC plc spends $10 million developing a new product, and the spending meets IFRS's tests for capitalisation. Under IAS 38 it records a $10 million intangible asset and, amortising it over 5 years, expenses $2 million a year. Under US GAAP most of that development spending would be expensed at once, cutting first-year profit by the full $10 million.

short: The accounting rules US companies use for their financial statements, written by the Financial Accounting Standards Board and enforced by the SEC.
kid: In one big country, every lemonade stand writes down its coins using the same rule book. That way anyone can compare the stands fairly.
detail: US Generally Accepted Accounting Principles (US GAAP) are the accounting standards that US public companies must follow in filings with the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC). They are written by the Financial Accounting Standards Board (FASB), a private body the SEC recognises, and since 2009 have been organised in a single Accounting Standards Codification, with topics such as ASC 606 on revenue and ASC 842 on leases. US GAAP is often described as more rules-based than IFRS, with detailed industry guidance. Key differences include allowing LIFO inventory costing, banning reversals of most impairment losses, and expensing most research and development. Indian subsidiaries of US companies report US GAAP numbers to their parents. The common confusion: 'GAAP' on its own just means a country's accepted accounting rules, so Indian GAAP and US GAAP differ, and non-GAAP figures are company-chosen measures outside these rules.
example: Say ABC Inc buys 100 units at $10 and then 100 units at $12, and sells 100 units at $15 each. Under FIFO, allowed by both US GAAP and IFRS, cost of goods sold is $1,000 and gross profit $500. Under LIFO, allowed only by US GAAP, cost is $1,200 and gross profit $300, which lowers taxable profit when prices are rising.

short: The auditor's formal conclusion on whether a company's financial statements give a true and fair view: clean, qualified, adverse or disclaimed.
kid: After a grown-up checks your piggy bank count, they say 'all correct', 'correct except one thing', 'quite wrong', or 'I could not check'.
detail: The audit opinion is the key paragraph of the independent auditor's report. An unmodified (unqualified, or clean) opinion says the financial statements present a true and fair view in all material respects. A qualified opinion says they do, except for a specific material issue, such as unsupported receivables. An adverse opinion says misstatements are so material and widespread that the statements are not true and fair. A disclaimer of opinion means the auditor could not gather enough evidence to form any view. In India these follow Standards on Auditing SA 700 and SA 705, which mirror the international ISA standards; a report may also carry an emphasis of matter, a going-concern warning or key audit matters, none of which by itself modifies the opinion. Listed companies must disclose the impact of any qualification. The common confusion: a clean opinion does not guarantee there is no fraud.
example: Say ABC Ltd reports profit of ₹40 crore, but its auditor finds ₹8 crore of receivables are unlikely to be collected and management refuses to write them off. Because the problem is material but confined to one item, the auditor gives a qualified opinion; ignoring tax, profit after the write-off would be ₹32 crore, 20% lower.

short: The independent chartered accountant or firm appointed by shareholders to audit a company's annual financial statements, as the law requires.
kid: Each year, the club picks a trusted grown-up from outside to count its coins and tell everyone whether the count is honest.
detail: A statutory auditor is the external auditor the law requires to examine a company's financial statements and report to shareholders. In India, under Sections 139 to 148 of the Companies Act, 2013, the auditor must be a chartered accountant or a firm of them, is appointed at the AGM for a five-year term, and can be removed early only with a special resolution and government approval. As of 2025, listed and larger companies must rotate an individual auditor after one term and an audit firm after two, with a five-year cooling-off. Auditors may not provide services such as internal audit or investment advice to audit clients. The Big Four firms (Deloitte, PwC, EY and KPMG) audit most of the world's largest companies. A mid-term resignation is a classic red flag, and SEBI requires its reasons to be disclosed. The common confusion: statutory and internal auditors are different people.
example: Say ABC Ltd, a listed company, appointed audit firm XYZ & Co at its 2016 AGM. After two five-year terms ending at the 2026 AGM, XYZ must step down and cannot audit ABC again until the 2031 AGM, once its five-year cooling-off is over.

short: A detailed investigation of a company's records to find, prove and measure fraud or misuse of money, often for use in court.
kid: If coins keep vanishing from the class jar, a detective looks at every note and every coin to find out exactly where they went and who took them.
detail: A forensic audit is an investigation, not a routine audit. It examines transactions, documents, emails and fund flows to detect and measure fraud, diversion of funds or other wrongdoing, with findings strong enough to support legal action. Specialists trace money through bank accounts, related companies and shell entities, and interview staff. In India, lenders commonly order forensic audits when a large borrower turns into a bad loan, and banks rely on them before classifying an account as fraud; SEBI and stock exchanges can also appoint forensic auditors for listed companies, which must disclose when one begins under the LODR rules. Collapses such as IL&FS, DHFL and Jet Airways all led to forensic audits. The common confusion: a statutory audit samples records to give an opinion on the accounts as a whole; a forensic audit hunts for specific misconduct and may check every transaction in an area.
example: Say lenders to ABC Ltd order a forensic audit after it defaults. The auditor finds ₹250 crore paid as advances to 12 suppliers, and 9 of them, which received ₹180 crore, share an address with the promoter's office and never delivered goods. That ₹180 crore, 72% of the advances, is flagged as likely diversion of funds.

short: Deliberately falsifying a company's financial statements, for example by inventing sales or hiding debts, to mislead investors and lenders.
kid: Imagine a child who tells everyone her piggy bank holds twenty coins when it really holds five, so friends keep lending her toys. Pretending to have more is cheating.
detail: Accounting fraud is the intentional misstatement of financial statements. Common methods are recording fake or early revenue, inflating assets such as cash, inventory or receivables, hiding liabilities off the balance sheet, capitalising ordinary expenses and manipulating provisions to smooth profit. Milder practices, called creative accounting, window dressing or earnings management, use aggressive but arguable choices; they become fraud when they cross into deception. In 2009 Satyam Computer Services' founder admitted that about ₹5,040 crore of cash and bank balances on its books did not exist, and globally Enron (2001) and Wirecard (2020) collapsed after similar revelations. Warning signs include profit rising while operating cash flow lags, receivables growing faster than sales, frequent auditor changes and heavy related-party dealings. The common confusion: a restatement to fix an honest error is not fraud; fraud requires intent to deceive.
example: Say ABC Ltd books ₹50 crore of sales in March for goods it ships only in April, lifting reported annual revenue from ₹500 crore to ₹550 crore. The 10% jump looks like growth, but receivables swell by the same ₹50 crore while operating cash flow does not move, a classic warning sign.

short: Global banking rules, agreed after the 2008 crisis, that require banks to hold more and better capital and enough easy-to-sell assets.
kid: A sweet shop keeps a big jar of spare sweets in case lots of children come at once or some sweets go bad. Grown-up rules say how big that spare jar must be.
detail: Basel III is the set of international banking standards agreed by the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, which meets at the Bank for International Settlements in Basel, in response to the 2008 global financial crisis. It raised the quality and amount of capital banks must hold against risk-weighted assets, with a minimum common equity tier 1 ratio of 4.5%, total capital of 8% and a 2.5% capital conservation buffer, plus extra buffers for systemically important banks. It also added a leverage ratio and two liquidity rules, the liquidity coverage ratio and the net stable funding ratio. The final 2017 reforms, nicknamed Basel IV, change how risk weights are calculated; their US version is called the Basel III endgame. As of 2025 the RBI sets stricter minimums than the global floor. The common confusion: the Basel Committee has no legal power; its standards bind only when national regulators adopt them.
example: Say XYZ Bank, a hypothetical lender, has risk-weighted assets of ₹2,00,000 crore. Basel III's global floor of 4.5% common equity tier 1 plus the 2.5% conservation buffer means at least 7%, or ₹14,000 crore, of core equity. The RBI's stricter 5.5% plus 2.5%, as of 2025, raises that to 8%, or ₹16,000 crore.
formula: Capital ratio = Regulatory capital / Risk-weighted assets

short: The sweeping 2010 US law that overhauled financial regulation after the 2008 crisis, from bank capital to derivatives and consumer protection.
kid: After a big mess at the playground, the grown-ups wrote a long list of new rules so the big kids could not take wild chances and knock everyone over again.
detail: The Dodd-Frank Wall Street Reform and Consumer Protection Act, signed in July 2010, is the main US legislative response to the 2008 financial crisis. It created the Financial Stability Oversight Council to watch for systemic risk, the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, and a process to wind down failing giant firms without taxpayer bailouts. It pushed most standardised over-the-counter derivatives into central clearing, required stress tests for large banks, and introduced the Volcker Rule, which limits banks' proprietary trading and their investments in hedge funds and private equity funds. It also brought in say-on-pay votes, whistle-blower rewards and pay clawbacks. A 2018 law eased several rules for smaller and mid-sized banks. The common confusion: Dodd-Frank did not break up big banks or restore the Glass-Steagall separation of commercial and investment banking; the Volcker Rule is a narrower restriction.
example: Say a whistle-blower's tip leads the SEC to collect $50 million in penalties from a hypothetical company. Under Dodd-Frank's programme, sanctions above $1 million qualify for an award of 10% to 30% of the amount collected, so the whistle-blower could receive between $5 million and $15 million.

short: A 2002 US law, passed after the Enron and WorldCom scandals, that tightened corporate financial reporting, internal controls and the oversight of auditors.
kid: After some children lied about how many sweets they had, the teacher made a rule: class leaders must sign a promise that their count is true, and someone checks the counting.
detail: The Sarbanes-Oxley Act of 2002 (SOX) is a US law passed after accounting frauds at Enron and WorldCom destroyed investor trust. It created the Public Company Accounting Oversight Board (PCAOB) to regulate auditors of public companies, barred auditors from providing many consulting services to audit clients, and required audit committees made up of independent directors. Section 302 makes the CEO and CFO personally certify each periodic report, and Section 906 adds criminal penalties for knowingly false certification. Section 404 requires management to assess internal control over financial reporting and, for larger companies, an auditor's attestation, the costliest part of SOX compliance. SOX applies to all companies listed in the US, including Indian firms with US listings, and India's Companies Act, 2013 and LODR rules borrow several of its ideas. The common confusion: SOX is about corporate reporting and audit, not banking rules like Dodd-Frank.
example: Say ABC Inc, a US-listed company, reports pre-tax profit of $80 million and its auditor sets materiality at 5%, or $4 million. A control gap lets $6 million of unsupported sales be booked; because that exceeds $4 million, it would likely be reported as a material weakness under Section 404, and the CEO and CFO must disclose it alongside their certifications.
